lld-logger-pubsub:0.prompt: A logger's minimum level is set to WARN, with levels DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR < FATAL. Which messages are emitted?
options: Only WARN
DEBUG and INFO
Everything, with WARN and above highlighted
WARN, ERROR and FATAL
lld-logger-pubsub:0.explanation: The minimum level is a threshold: messages at that severity or higher pass, lower ones are dropped. It is not an exact-match filter, which is why setting WARN still surfaces errors.
Only levels with a numeric value ≥ 30 pass, so error:b and warn:c are kept in call order. Numeric levels make the threshold a single comparison, the approach pino and winston use.

lld-logger-pubsub:0.prompt: You need to add an HTTP sink that ships logs to a collector, alongside the console and file sinks, without modifying the Logger class. Which design allows that?
options: Logger holds a list of objects implementing a Sink interface (write(record)) and calls each one
Logger has a switch on a sinkType string with one case per destination
Each call site decides where to write and calls fs or fetch directly
Logger extends FileLogger, which extends ConsoleLogger, adding one level per sink
lld-logger-pubsub:0.explanation: Depending on a Sink abstraction lets you register new destinations (console, file, HTTP, test spy) without touching Logger. A switch must be edited for each new sink, and an inheritance chain can't mix sinks freely.

lld-logger-pubsub:0.prompt: Profiling shows `logger.debug('state: ' + JSON.stringify(hugeState))` is costly even though production runs at INFO. Why, and what is the fix?
options: debug() still writes to disk at INFO level; disable the file sink
The argument is built before debug() is called; check isLevelEnabled('debug') first or pass a function evaluated lazily
JSON.stringify is cached between calls; clear the cache
The logger is synchronous; switching to console.debug avoids the cost
lld-logger-pubsub:0.explanation: JavaScript evaluates arguments eagerly, so the expensive string is built and then discarded by the level check. Guarding with a level check, passing a thunk, or passing the object for the logger to serialize only if enabled avoids the work.

lld-logger-pubsub:0.prompt: A Node.js service writes every log line with fs.appendFileSync. Under load, p99 latency rises sharply. What is the cause and the usual remedy?
options: appendFileSync opens a new thread per call; use a thread pool
The file grows too big; rotate it every hour
Synchronous writes block the event loop; buffer and write asynchronously (e.g. a worker-thread transport), flushing on shutdown
Log lines are too long; truncate them to 80 characters
lld-logger-pubsub:0.explanation: Every sync write stalls all requests on the event loop. Async/buffered writers or worker transports (as pino does) move that cost off the hot path; the trade-off is that a hard crash may lose the last buffered lines, so flush on exit signals. Rotation doesn't change per-write blocking.

lld-logger-pubsub:0.prompt: Why do production services emit structured (JSON) logs with fields like level, msg, requestId and durationMs instead of free-form strings?
options: JSON is smaller on disk than plain text
Free-form strings can't contain timestamps
Structured logs don't need a log level
Aggregators can filter and aggregate by field (e.g. all errors for one requestId) without fragile regex parsing
lld-logger-pubsub:0.explanation: Fields make logs queryable: count errors by route, trace a requestId, chart durations. JSON is usually larger than plain text, and levels and timestamps remain essential fields.

lld-logger-pubsub:0.prompt: You want every log line written while handling a request to include that request's ID, even deep inside async helpers that never receive the ID as a parameter. Which Node.js feature fits?
options: A module-level variable set at the start of each request
AsyncLocalStorage, which carries a store through the async calls started from a request
process.env.REQUEST_ID, set per request
A WeakMap keyed by the current function
lld-logger-pubsub:0.explanation: AsyncLocalStorage propagates context across awaits, timers and callbacks started within run(). A module-level variable or env var is shared by all concurrent requests, so interleaved requests overwrite each other's ID.

lld-logger-pubsub:0.prompt: Which of these should never appear in application logs? Select all that apply.
options: User passwords, even when a login fails
Full card numbers
Request IDs
Session tokens and API keys
HTTP status codes
lld-logger-pubsub:0.explanation: Secrets and card data in logs turn the log store into a breach target and violate PCI-DSS. Request IDs and status codes are exactly what logs are for. Redaction at the logger (e.g. configured redact paths) is safer than relying on every call site.

lld-logger-pubsub:0.prompt: Which statements about a shared logger instance in a Node.js app are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Exporting one instance from a module makes it effectively a singleton, because modules are cached
A hard-wired global logger makes tests harder unless sinks or the instance can be injected
Child loggers with bound context, e.g. logger.child({ requestId }), avoid repeating fields at every call
A singleton logger is unsafe because worker threads share the same module instance and can corrupt it
lld-logger-pubsub:0.explanation: Module caching gives one instance per process (per realm), which is convenient but needs an injection seam for tests; child loggers add context cheaply. Worker threads each load their own module instances, so they don't share the singleton.

lld-logger-pubsub:0.prompt: If one sink, such as a remote HTTP collector, is slow or down, a well-designed logger should keep it from blocking or crashing the request path.
options: True
False
lld-logger-pubsub:0.explanation: Logging is a side concern: a failing sink should be isolated with async buffering, bounded queues, timeouts and error handling, dropping or spilling logs rather than taking down the service.

lld-logger-pubsub:0.prompt: Setting the logger level to ERROR means ERROR messages and all lower-severity messages such as INFO are emitted.
options: True
False
lld-logger-pubsub:0.explanation: The level is a minimum severity: ERROR emits ERROR and above (e.g. FATAL) and suppresses INFO, DEBUG and WARN. Setting a lower level like DEBUG is what makes everything visible.

lld-logger-pubsub:1.prompt: What is the core data structure of a simple in-memory pub-sub broker?
options: A single array of all messages that every subscriber scans
A priority queue ordered by message size
A map from topic name to a collection of subscriber callbacks or queues
A linked list of topics where each topic points to the next publisher
lld-logger-pubsub:1.explanation: publish(topic, msg) looks up the topic's subscribers and delivers to each; subscribe and unsubscribe add to or remove from that collection. Scanning one global array makes every publish O(all messages).

A unsubscribes itself during the first publish; deleting the current element from a Set during iteration is safe and B still runs. The second publish only reaches B, and topic 'y' has no subscribers (?? [] avoids a crash).

Set iteration is live: an element added during a for...of is visited later in the same loop, so the subscriber added mid-publish receives the current message. Brokers often iterate over a snapshot ([...subs]) to avoid this.

lld-logger-pubsub:1.prompt: In a synchronous in-memory broker, one subscriber does a slow 200 ms computation per message, and publishers start timing out. What is the best fix?
options: Give each subscriber its own queue and deliver asynchronously, so publish only enqueues
Raise the publishers' timeout to 500 ms
Call the slow subscriber last so the others aren't delayed
Convert the slow subscriber to an async function without changing the broker
lld-logger-pubsub:1.explanation: Decoupling via per-subscriber queues makes publish O(subscribers) enqueues and isolates slow consumers (with bounded queues and backpressure or drop policies). Reordering still blocks the publisher, and making a CPU-bound handler async doesn't free the event loop.

lld-logger-pubsub:1.prompt: In a naive broker, publish loops over subscribers and calls each one. A subscriber throws. What happens, and what should the broker do?
options: The exception is ignored automatically by for...of
Later subscribers don't get the message; wrap each call in try/catch and report the error
The message is re-delivered to every subscriber until none throws
The throwing subscriber is unsubscribed automatically by JavaScript
lld-logger-pubsub:1.explanation: An exception aborts the loop and propagates to the publisher, so one buggy consumer breaks delivery for everyone after it. Isolate each delivery, log or route failures (e.g. to a dead-letter list) and keep going.

lld-logger-pubsub:1.prompt: Topic 'orders' has consumer group 'billing' with 3 instances and consumer group 'email' with 2 instances. How many deliveries does one published message produce under standard group semantics?
options: 5, one per instance
1, to a random instance
3, one per billing instance
2, one per group
lld-logger-pubsub:1.explanation: Each group receives every message, but within a group only one instance processes it (competing consumers), so one delivery per group. Broadcasting to all 5 instances would make billing charge three times.

lld-logger-pubsub:1.prompt: You want a consumer that was offline for an hour to catch up on missed messages, while other consumers keep their own pace. Which design supports this?
options: Delete each message as soon as the first consumer acknowledges it
Push messages only to currently connected consumers
Store each topic as an append-only log and keep a committed offset per consumer group
Keep only the latest message per topic
lld-logger-pubsub:1.explanation: With a retained log, each group reads from its own offset, so a returning consumer resumes where it stopped (subject to retention). Deleting on first ack or push-only delivery loses the messages the offline consumer needed. This is the Kafka-style model.

lld-logger-pubsub:1.prompt: Which statements about delivery semantics are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Acknowledging after processing gives at-least-once delivery, so duplicates are possible
Acknowledging before processing gives at-most-once delivery, so messages can be lost on a crash
At-least-once delivery requires idempotent consumers to be safe
A purely in-memory broker keeps undelivered messages across a process restart
lld-logger-pubsub:1.explanation: When you ack decides what a crash costs: ack-late risks redelivery, ack-early risks loss, and idempotency makes redelivery harmless. Anything held only in memory is gone after a restart unless persisted.

lld-logger-pubsub:1.prompt: Which practices prevent memory leaks in an in-memory pub-sub? Select all that apply.
options: Return an unsubscribe function from subscribe() and call it when the consumer is done
Bound per-subscriber queues and apply a drop or backpressure policy for slow consumers
Remove a topic's entry when its last subscriber leaves
Store subscribers in a WeakMap keyed by topic string
lld-logger-pubsub:1.explanation: Leaks come from forgotten subscriptions, unbounded queues and empty topic entries. WeakMap keys must be objects, not strings, and weak references wouldn't help anyway, since the broker itself holds the callbacks.

lld-logger-pubsub:1.prompt: Node.js EventEmitter calls listeners synchronously, in the order they were registered, when emit() is called.
options: True
False
lld-logger-pubsub:1.explanation: emit() runs each listener inline before returning, so a slow or throwing listener affects the emitter. Listeners that need async work must schedule it themselves (e.g. setImmediate or queueMicrotask).

lld-logger-pubsub:1.prompt: With 3 consumers in a single competing-consumers group, every message is delivered to all 3 consumers.
options: True
False
lld-logger-pubsub:1.explanation: Competing consumers share the work: each message goes to exactly one member of the group, which is how you scale processing. Fan-out to everyone is what separate groups (or plain broadcast subscribers) provide.

lld-logger-pubsub:2.prompt: Which data structure is the standard core of an in-memory delayed task scheduler?
options: A min-heap ordered by run time: O(log n) insert, O(1) peek at the next task
An unsorted array scanned on every tick
A hash map keyed by task ID
A FIFO queue in insertion order
lld-logger-pubsub:2.explanation: The scheduler always needs the earliest task next, which a min-heap provides cheaply. A FIFO only works if tasks are inserted in run-time order, and a hash map has no ordering (though it's often added for lookup by ID).

lld-logger-pubsub:2.prompt: In Node.js, what happens with `setTimeout(fn, 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)` (30 days)?
options: fn runs after 30 days, as requested
It throws a RangeError immediately
The delay exceeds the 32-bit timer limit (~24.8 days), so Node warns and runs fn after about 1 ms
The timer is silently ignored and fn never runs
lld-logger-pubsub:2.explanation: Delays above 2^31 − 1 ms trigger a TimeoutOverflowWarning and are set to 1 ms. Long-delay schedulers therefore keep tasks in a heap or database and only arm a timer for the nearest one, capped below the limit.

Tasks are ordered by time, and Array.prototype.sort is stable (guaranteed since ES2019), so email stays ahead of cleanup at the same time. All four are due at 300. Sorting on each insert is O(n log n), which is why real schedulers use a heap.

Timers fire in order of due time, and timers with the same delay fire in the order they were created, so a (10 ms) runs first, then b and c (20 ms) in creation order. The 30 ms timer logs after all three.

lld-logger-pubsub:2.prompt: A scheduler keeps tasks in a min-heap and arms a single setTimeout for the earliest task. A new task is scheduled to run before the current earliest. What must happen?
options: Nothing; the new task will be found when the existing timer fires
Arm a second timer just for the new task and keep both
Rebuild the heap from scratch so the timer picks up the change
Clear the current timer and re-arm it for the new task's run time
lld-logger-pubsub:2.explanation: The single timer must always target the heap's head. If you don't re-arm, the new task runs late (when the old timer fires). Arming a timer per task defeats the purpose of the single-timer design.

lld-logger-pubsub:2.prompt: A report job is scheduled every 60 s but sometimes takes 70 s. With fixed-rate scheduling (next run based on the previous start time), what happens, compared with fixed-delay (next run 60 s after the previous finishes)?
options: Fixed-rate runs can overlap or pile up; fixed-delay never overlaps but drifts later over time
Fixed-delay runs overlap; fixed-rate always waits for completion
Both behave identically when the job takes longer than the interval
Fixed-rate skips the job permanently after one overrun
lld-logger-pubsub:2.explanation: Fixed-rate keeps the cadence, so a slow run means the next one is already due (overlap, or a backlog if runs are serialized). Fixed-delay waits for completion, avoiding overlap but shifting the schedule. Pick based on whether cadence or exclusivity matters.

lld-logger-pubsub:2.prompt: Your in-memory scheduler loses all pending tasks on every deploy. Which PostgreSQL-backed design lets several workers run due tasks durably without running a task twice at the same time?
options: Each worker runs SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE run_at <= now() and executes everything it gets
Workers claim tasks with SELECT ... WHERE run_at <= now() ORDER BY run_at LIMIT n FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, then mark them taken
Store tasks in a JSON file on each worker's local disk
Use one worker only and keep a setTimeout per task loaded at boot
lld-logger-pubsub:2.explanation: SKIP LOCKED lets concurrent workers claim disjoint batches without blocking each other, and persisting tasks survives restarts. A plain SELECT lets every worker run the same tasks, and a single worker with timers is a single point of failure.

lld-logger-pubsub:2.prompt: How can a heap-based scheduler support cancel(taskId)? Select all that apply.
options: Mark the task as cancelled (lazy deletion) and skip it when it reaches the top of the heap
Keep a map from task ID to heap index so the task can be removed in O(log n)
Cancellation is impossible once a task is in a binary heap
With lazy deletion, cancelled entries still occupy memory until popped, so many cancellations may call for periodic compaction
lld-logger-pubsub:2.explanation: Lazy deletion is simple and O(1) to cancel, at the cost of tombstones in the heap; an index map allows true O(log n) removal by sifting. Both are standard, so cancellation is very much possible.

lld-logger-pubsub:2.prompt: Which concerns apply when a Node.js scheduler executes its tasks? Select all that apply.
options: A CPU-heavy task on the main thread delays every other timer
Limit how many async tasks run at once, e.g. with a concurrency pool
Timers guarantee a task runs at exactly its scheduled millisecond
Catch task errors and rejections so one failing task doesn't crash the process
lld-logger-pubsub:2.explanation: Timers are 'not before' guarantees: a busy event loop makes them late. Long CPU work belongs in worker threads, concurrency limits protect downstream systems, and an unhandled rejection crashes Node by default.

lld-logger-pubsub:2.prompt: In Node.js, setTimeout(fn, 100) means fn will not run earlier than about 100 ms later, but it can run later if the event loop is busy.
options: True
False
lld-logger-pubsub:2.explanation: The delay is a minimum: the callback runs in the timers phase once the time has elapsed and the loop gets there. Long synchronous work or a backlog of callbacks pushes it later.

lld-logger-pubsub:2.prompt: Keeping tasks in a sorted array gives O(log n) insertion, because binary search finds the right position.
options: True
False
lld-logger-pubsub:2.explanation: Binary search finds the position in O(log n), but inserting into an array shifts later elements, which is O(n). A heap gives O(log n) insertion and removal of the minimum.
